video_title: Live from Emory Law: Stacey Abrams joins Alex Bores & Kevin Frazier
gist: At a live Emory Law taping of Lawfare's Scaling Laws, Stacey Abrams argues the US is in 'competitive authoritarianism' but that '10 steps to freedom and power' can reverse it, and lays out an AI governance agenda: state/local regulation, children's data protections, public AI, and compensating data creators. She criticizes AI labs (Amodei's essay, a reported Sherman Act exemption request), describes AI civic and legal tools she has built, and co-host Alex Bores opposes federal preemption that bars state AI laws.

themes.theme: US democratic backsliding and the '10 steps' frame

insights.claim: Abrams characterizes the US as being in a state of 'competitive authoritarianism', with fewer active democracies worldwide today than 20 years ago, and says a 20-year 'hitchhiker' using democratic institutions for authoritarian ends turned into 'hijacking' last year.
insights.speaker: Stacey Abrams
insights.so_what: Signals a durable institutional-risk framing that Democrats will campaign and govern on.
insights.quote: we are as a nation in the midst of what's referred to as competitive authoritarianism.

insights.claim: Abrams argues every modern authoritarian (Bolsonaro, Orban, Putin, Modi, Erdogan) followed the same 10 steps, but reversals in Serbia, Nepal and South Korea show there are equally '10 steps to freedom and power'.
insights.speaker: Stacey Abrams
insights.so_what: Frames US backsliding as reversible, informing political-risk scenarios.

insights.claim: Abrams cautions against direct Hungary-US analogies because Hungary's 10 million people is 'basically traffic on I85', so lessons from Peter Magyar defeating Orban transfer only partially.
insights.speaker: Stacey Abrams
insights.so_what: Foreign opposition playbooks may not map to the US scale.
insights.quote: Hungary has 10 million people that's basically traffic on I85

insights.claim: Abrams lists step seven (scapegoating vulnerable groups, which in the US is labeled 'DEI') and step nine (normalized state violence, citing the capital under military occupation for more than a year) as signs of advanced authoritarian drift, with step 10 being the SAVE Act.
insights.speaker: Stacey Abrams
insights.so_what: Expect voting-access legislation like the SAVE Act to be a central partisan battleground.

insights.claim: Abrams argues that Americans' self-image as a born democracy creates normalization bias and denial that makes it harder to recognize authoritarian slide.
insights.speaker: Stacey Abrams
insights.so_what: Public complacency can delay political correction, extending policy-risk regimes.

insights.claim: Abrams' 10 Steps campaign has more than 120 partner organizations and over 250,000 sign-ups, and is building an AI civic coach called 'Marion' that maps users to bespoke civic actions.
insights.speaker: Stacey Abrams
insights.so_what: Shows AI being deployed as mass political-organizing infrastructure.
insights.quote: We've got more than 120 organizations. More than 250,000 people have signed up with us.

themes.theme: AI governance: labs, preemption, and public AI

insights.claim: Abrams says the US is woefully behind other nations, including China, in passing AI law, and that state and local governments are currently the only entities regulating AI at scale.
insights.speaker: Stacey Abrams
insights.so_what: State-level AI regulation is the live regulatory risk for AI companies.
insights.quote: even those who can point out the harms are unwilling to entertain the solution sets.

insights.claim: Abrams criticizes Dario Amodei's lengthy essay for calling to slow AI development but not data center development or to speed state and local oversight.
insights.speaker: Stacey Abrams
insights.so_what: Political pressure is shifting toward data center siting and local oversight.
insights.quote: He said slow down the development of the AI, not the development of data centers.

insights.claim: Abrams claims that while the lab's essay was published, AI firms quietly asked Congress for an exemption from the Sherman Antitrust Act.
insights.speaker: Stacey Abrams
insights.so_what: Antitrust treatment of AI labs is an emerging policy flashpoint.
insights.quote: they also quietly went to Congress to ask to be exempted from the Sherman Antitrust Act.

insights.claim: Abrams' five-year vision for AI governance includes federal/state/local laws, children's data protections (e.g., school Chromebooks), international standards, public AI to counter oligarchic control, and compensation for people whose data built the models.
insights.speaker: Stacey Abrams
insights.so_what: Data-compensation and public-AI demands could reshape AI cost structures if Democrats gain power.

insights.claim: Abrams says eight of her books were scraped and she is part of the Anthropic settlement, arguing data creators should be paid and that this is a solvable moral, not money, problem.
insights.speaker: Stacey Abrams
insights.so_what: Copyright settlements are setting a precedent for creator compensation.
insights.quote: I'm I'm in the anthropic settlement, so I have eight books that they've got to pay me back for.

insights.claim: Assembly member Alex Bores, author of the RAISE Act, says he would trade it for a federal rule but opposes an 'anti-democracy clause' barring states from enforcing any new AI laws.
insights.speaker: Alex Bores
insights.so_what: Federal preemption fights will determine whether state AI laws survive.
insights.quote: I would happily trade it for a federal rule versus what I call an anti-democracy clause

insights.claim: Abrams is training a roughly 150-person, low-income, largely agricultural South Georgia town on AI because its county is a likely data center target that she says threatens residents' jobs, water and power bills.
insights.speaker: Stacey Abrams
insights.so_what: Grassroots opposition to data centers over water and power costs is organizing in target counties.
insights.quote: Their county is likely going to be a target of a data center.

themes.theme: AI as tool, not decision-maker; access to justice

insights.claim: Abrams' American Pride Rises built 'Adiva', its own LLM trained only on trusted sources, which helped thousands of small organizations interpret anti-DEI rules when lawyers were afraid to answer, though she says it still needs human intercessors.
insights.speaker: Stacey Abrams
insights.so_what: Narrow, trusted-source legal LLMs can close access-to-justice gaps.

insights.claim: Abrams argues AI can mimic objectivity well enough to reveal human bias in sentencing, but decisions like sentencing should remain human because of context and nuance.
insights.speaker: Stacey Abrams
insights.so_what: Expect resistance to fully automated judicial decision-making.
insights.quote: AI is not actually objective but it can mimic objectivity sufficient ly to reveal our biases.

insights.claim: Abrams says AI is a generator of alternative solution sets and an ideator but should never be the decision-maker, and she uses multiple LLM personas to test her own thinking.
insights.speaker: Stacey Abrams
insights.so_what: Positioning AI as augmentation rather than automation shapes public acceptance.
insights.quote: technology is a great generator of alternative solution sets. It can never be the decision maker

insights.claim: Kevin Frazier argues lawyers have a duty to improve access to justice and should not use unauthorized-practice-of-law rules to block new legal tools.
insights.speaker: Kevin Frazier
insights.so_what: Legal-profession guild rules are a regulatory barrier to legal AI adoption.
